summary: Provides test vectors for PKCS #5's PBKDF2 using HMAC-SHA-1 so implementers can check their code. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives sample inputs and expected outputs for PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-1. Implementers can use the examples to check whether their code computes the same values.

questions: what inputs are in the pbkdf2 test vectors
how can i test pbkdf2 hmac sha1
subtitle: Known input and output values for PBKDF2 using HMAC-SHA-1.

tldr.problem: Implementers needed test vectors for PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-1 because the original specification did not include them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists six password, salt, iteration-count, and output-length inputs with their expected derived keys.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can compare their computed outputs with the published values to test their implementation.

today: RFC 6070 is an Informational collection of PBKDF2 HMAC-SHA-1 test vectors. The unit metadata lists no update or replacement.

sections.title: Why the Test Vectors Are Provided
sections.content:
PBKDF2 is a password-based key derivation function defined by PKCS #5. The RFC says it is used by protocols to derive encryption keys from a password.

The original specification did not include test vectors, which are useful for implementers. RFC 6070 supplies examples for PBKDF2 using HMAC with SHA-1.
sections.plainLanguage: A test vector gives known inputs and the expected answer. These examples let programmers compare their PBKDF2 output with the RFC.

sections.title: Inputs and Expected Derived Keys
sections.content:
Each vector gives a password, salt, iteration count, and requested derived-key length. The RFC includes cases with one, two, 4096, and 16777216 iterations, as well as longer inputs and embedded NUL characters.

Expected derived keys are shown in hexadecimal. The RFC says the input strings are ASCII and defines \0 as a literal ASCII NUL octet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each example lists the password, salt, and settings, then gives the exact key bytes to expect. One example checks how the implementation handles NUL characters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the security considerations in RFC 2898 apply. It introduces no new security considerations of its own.

The document is a collection of test vectors, not a new definition of PBKDF2 behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo adds examples rather than a new cryptographic algorithm. It points readers to RFC 2898 for the security considerations.

references.text: Kaliski, B., "PKCS #5: Password-Based Cryptography Specification Version 2.0", RFC 2898, September 2000.
Krawczyk, H., Bellare, M., and R. Canetti, "HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication", RFC 2104, February 1997.
